passage.text_en:
Plants are remarkable organisms that have evolved unique cellular structures to thrive in environments where they cannot move. Unlike animal cells, plant cells possess a rigid cell wall composed primarily of cellulose, which provides structural support and protection.

Within the plant cell, chloroplasts serve as the sites of photosynthesis. These organelles contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light energy and converts it into chemical energy. Through photosynthesis, plants produce glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct.

Another critical structure in plant cells is the central vacuole, a large fluid-filled sac that can occupy up to 90% of the cell volume. The vacuole stores water, nutrients, and waste products. It also helps maintain turgor pressure, which keeps plants rigid and upright.

Scientists believe that the evolution of these specialized structures occurred over billions of years. Early plants developed simple chloroplasts through a process called endosymbiosis.
